paper_title: On the Suitability of Syndrome Decoding for Proof-of-Work under Quantum Adversaries: Design and Analysis
authors: Aleck Nash, Kim-Kwang Raymond Choo, and Henry Chimal-Dzul
statement: results are based on random-instance assumptions and approximate independence heuristics commonly used in decoding complexity analyses. While these assumptions are widely used in the literature, they do not constitute formal guarantees. Additionally, our proposed construction does not eliminate the quantum advantage: existing quantum ISD algorithms still yield a non-negligible speedup. Our contribution is to quantify this gap and to show that it differs from that of unstructured search. Moreover, the effect of the profile constraint depends on how decoding algorithms interact with structured solution spaces. Our analysis captures the baseline setting in which this structure is not fully exploited. However, the extent to which it can be leveraged algorithmically remains open. Finally, our comparisons are asymptotic and based on exponent-level models, and should be interpreted as comparative indicators rather than exact runtime predictions.
context: 7. CONCLUDING REMARKS 15 results are based on random-instance assumptions and approximate independence heuristics commonly used in decoding complexity analyses. While these assumptions are widely used in the literature, they do not constitute formal guarantees. Additionally, our proposed construction does not eliminate the quantum advantage: existing quantum ISD algorithms still yield a non-negligible speedup. Our contribution is to quantify this gap and to show that it differs from that of unstructured search. Moreover, the effect of the profile constraint depends on how decoding algorithms interact with structured solution spaces. Our analysis captures the baseline setting in which this structure is not fully exploited. However, the extent to which it can be leveraged algorithmically remains open. Finally, our comparisons are asymptotic and based on exponent-level models, and should be interpreted as comparative indicators rather than exact runtime predictions. Future work. Several directions remain open. In particular, it is important to un- derstand how modern decoding algorithms can be adapted to exploit structured constraints, to evaluate concrete parameter choices in practice, and to investigate alternative constructions that further shape the solution space. Additionally, this work focuses on the construction and decoding complexity of the underlying computational puzzle. A complete deployment in Nakamoto-style consensus would additionally require analysis of precomputation, possible cross-instance amortization, parallel scaling, and the distribution of block-generation times. These protocol-level questions are left for future work. These directions may lead to a more refined understanding of quantum advantage in structured proof-of-work systems.
